rules.title: A router or modem admin page is reachable from the internet
rules.explain: The page identifies itself as a router, modem or ISP gateway management interface. Admin pages on home gateways are a favourite target: default passwords, unpatched firmware and login bugs turn them into a takeover of the whole network.
rules.advice: Turn off remote/WAN management in the router settings (often called 'Remote Management', 'Web access from WAN' or '远程管理'). Manage it from inside the house or over a VPN.

rules.title: A camera or video recorder interface is reachable
rules.explain: The page looks like an IP camera, NVR or DVR. These devices are among the most frequently hijacked on the internet and expose live video of your home.
rules.advice: Remove the port forward/UPnP mapping for the camera. Use the vendor's cloud app or a VPN to watch remotely, change the default password and update the firmware.

rules.title: A server or hypervisor admin panel is reachable
rules.explain: The page looks like a server control panel (hypervisor, container manager, hosting panel or database web UI). Whoever gets past its login controls the machine and everything on it.
rules.advice: Do not publish admin panels. Bind them to the LAN and reach them over a VPN or Tailscale; if one must be public, put it behind an authenticating reverse proxy and enable 2FA.

rules.title: A NAS management interface is reachable
rules.explain: The page identifies a NAS (network storage) login. NAS boxes hold the family's files and photos and are the prime target of ransomware campaigns that scan for exactly these pages.
rules.advice: Prefer the vendor's relay (e.g. QuickConnect / myQNAPcloud) or a VPN over a direct port forward. If it stays public: HTTPS only, 2FA, auto-block on failed logins, and keep DSM/QTS updated.

rules.title: A home-automation interface is reachable
rules.explain: The page looks like a smart-home controller. It can switch locks, lights, alarms and cameras, so its login is effectively the key to the house.
rules.advice: Use the project's cloud relay or a VPN for remote access; if published, require HTTPS, strong passwords and 2FA, and keep it updated.

rules.title: A self-hosted application is reachable
rules.explain: The page identifies a self-hosted service (media server, download client, file sync). Publishing these is often deliberate, but download clients and sync tools frequently run with weak or no authentication.
rules.advice: If this is intentional, make sure it requires a login, runs over HTTPS and is kept up to date. Download clients (qBittorrent, Transmission, aria2) should not be public at all.

rules.title: An embedded device's web interface is reachable
rules.explain: The web server software is typical of routers, cameras and other appliances (not of a normal website). Appliance firmware is rarely patched; several of these servers have well-known remote-takeover bugs.
rules.advice: Find which device this is (the evidence below helps) and remove its port forward or UPnP mapping; manage it from inside the network.

rules.title: A web interface is reachable over plain HTTP
rules.explain: Something serves web pages without encryption. Anything typed into it — including passwords — crosses the internet in the clear.
rules.advice: Identify it from the title/server evidence. If it is a device admin page, close it; if it is a site you publish, serve it over HTTPS and redirect HTTP.

rules.title: A web service is reachable over HTTPS
rules.explain: Something serves encrypted web pages here. The certificate and page title in the evidence are the best clue to what it is.
rules.advice: Confirm you meant to publish it. A self-signed certificate usually means a device admin page rather than a website — those should not be public.

rules.title: A common web port is open
rules.explain: This port is conventionally used for web interfaces, but the service did not answer an HTTP request clearly enough to identify it.
rules.advice: Open the address in a browser from outside to see what it is; remove the forward if it is not something you publish on purpose.

rules.title: A common HTTPS port is open
rules.explain: This port is conventionally used for HTTPS interfaces, but no TLS handshake or page could be read to identify it.
rules.advice: Open it in a browser from outside to see what it is; remove the forward if it is not deliberate.

rules.title: A login prompt sends the password unencrypted
rules.explain: The service asks for a username and password with HTTP Basic authentication over plain HTTP, so the password is readable by anyone on the path.
rules.advice: Close the port, or serve it over HTTPS only.

rules.title: The TLS certificate has expired
rules.explain: The certificate presented on this port is past its expiry date. Browsers will warn, and it often signals a forgotten, unmaintained service.
rules.advice: Renew the certificate (or switch to automatic renewal), or close the port if the service is no longer used.

rules.title: The TLS certificate is self-signed
rules.explain: A self-signed certificate is typical of device admin interfaces (routers, NAS, cameras) rather than published websites.
rules.advice: Use this as a clue to identify the device; if it is an admin interface, it should not face the internet.

rules.title: SSH is reachable from the internet
rules.explain: An SSH server answers here. It is constantly probed by password-guessing bots; it is safe only with key-only login and an up-to-date server.
rules.advice: Disable password login (keys only), disable root login, keep it updated — or reach it through a VPN/Tailscale and close the port.

rules.title: The SSH port is open
rules.explain: Port 22 is open, though no SSH greeting was read to confirm it.
rules.advice: If this is SSH: keys only, no root login, keep it updated, or move it behind a VPN.

rules.title: Telnet is exposed
rules.explain: Telnet is an unencrypted remote shell, typically on routers, modems and IoT devices. It is the classic entry point for botnets such as Mirai.
rules.advice: Disable Telnet on the device or block it on the router immediately; use SSH from inside the network if you need a shell.

rules.title: Windows Remote Desktop is exposed
rules.explain: RDP is one of the most attacked services on the internet and a common ransomware entry point.
rules.advice: Do not expose RDP directly; reach the PC through a VPN/Tailscale, or a remote-access tool with 2FA.

rules.title: VNC remote desktop is exposed
rules.explain: A VNC server answered. VNC passwords are short and often absent; exposed VNC screens are routinely found and taken over.
rules.advice: Close the port and reach the machine through a VPN or an SSH tunnel.

rules.title: A VNC port is open
rules.explain: A port conventionally used for VNC remote desktop is open.
rules.advice: If this is VNC, close it and use a VPN or SSH tunnel instead.

rules.title: Windows Remote Management is exposed
rules.explain: WinRM gives remote command execution on Windows machines.
rules.advice: Close the port; administer Windows hosts over a VPN.

rules.title: Android debugging (ADB) is exposed
rules.explain: ADB over the network gives full control of an Android device or TV box without a password. Exposed ADB is mass-exploited by crypto-mining and botnet malware.
rules.advice: Turn off network debugging on the device and remove the port forward/UPnP mapping.

rules.title: A MySQL/MariaDB database is exposed
rules.explain: The database greeted WanHound with its version. Databases facing the internet are brute-forced and wiped or ransomed within hours.
rules.advice: Bind the database to localhost/LAN only and reach it through an SSH tunnel or VPN.

rules.title: A database port (MySQL) is exposed
rules.explain: The standard MySQL port is open.
rules.advice: Bind the database to localhost/LAN only and reach it through an SSH tunnel or VPN.

rules.title: A database port (PostgreSQL) is exposed
rules.explain: The standard PostgreSQL port is open. Databases facing the internet are brute-forced and ransomed.
rules.advice: Restrict listen_addresses / pg_hba.conf to the LAN and use an SSH tunnel or VPN.

rules.title: Redis is exposed
rules.explain: Redis has no password by default; an exposed instance is routinely used to plant SSH keys and cron jobs, i.e. to take over the host.
rules.advice: Bind Redis to 127.0.0.1/LAN, enable protected-mode and a password, and remove the port forward.

rules.title: MongoDB is exposed
rules.explain: Exposed MongoDB instances are found by automated scanners and wiped for ransom.
rules.advice: Bind to localhost/LAN, enable authentication, and remove the port forward.

rules.title: Microsoft SQL Server is exposed
rules.explain: SQL Server facing the internet is a constant brute-force target.
rules.advice: Restrict it to the LAN and reach it over a VPN.

rules.title: Elasticsearch is exposed
rules.explain: Elasticsearch often runs without authentication; exposed clusters leak or lose their entire contents.
rules.advice: Bind it to the LAN, enable security features, and remove the port forward.

rules.title: CouchDB is exposed
rules.explain: CouchDB's HTTP API on the internet is a known target for data theft and cryptomining.
rules.advice: Bind it to the LAN and require authentication.

rules.title: memcached is exposed
rules.explain: memcached has no authentication and is abused for data leaks and huge DDoS amplification.
rules.advice: Bind memcached to localhost and remove the port forward.

rules.title: InfluxDB is exposed
rules.explain: Time-series databases often hold home-automation and monitoring data and are frequently deployed without auth.
rules.advice: Restrict it to the LAN or require authentication.

rules.title: ZooKeeper is exposed
rules.explain: ZooKeeper has no authentication by default and leaks configuration data.
rules.advice: Restrict it to the LAN.

rules.title: The Docker API is exposed without TLS
rules.explain: The unencrypted Docker API gives anyone root on the host: they can start a container that mounts your disk.
rules.advice: Close it now. Use the local socket, or SSH (`docker -H ssh://`) for remote management.

rules.title: The Docker TLS API port is open
rules.explain: Docker's TLS port is open. It is safe only if client-certificate verification is enforced.
rules.advice: Prefer SSH-based Docker access; if kept, verify --tlsverify is on and restrict source addresses.

rules.title: The Webmin port is open
rules.explain: Port 10000 is Webmin's default — a full system administration panel.
rules.advice: If this is Webmin, close it and use it over a VPN.

rules.title: A router management protocol (TR-069/CWMP) is exposed
rules.explain: TR-069 lets the ISP manage your router remotely. Its listener on the WAN side has been the target of large botnet campaigns.
rules.advice: If the router is yours, disable TR-069/CWMP; if it is the ISP's, ask them to restrict it to their management network and keep the firmware current.

rules.title: MikroTik Winbox management is exposed
rules.explain: Winbox is MikroTik's router management protocol and has a history of critical, mass-exploited vulnerabilities.
rules.advice: Restrict Winbox to LAN/VPN in IP → Services (available-from) and the firewall input chain; keep RouterOS updated.

rules.title: The MikroTik API is exposed
rules.explain: The RouterOS API allows full router configuration and is brute-forced like any login.
rules.advice: Disable the API service or restrict it to the LAN.

rules.title: SNMP is exposed
rules.explain: SNMP exposes device configuration and, with default community strings, can allow changes.
rules.advice: Disable SNMP on the WAN side.

rules.title: SMB file sharing is exposed
rules.explain: Windows/Samba file sharing was the vector of WannaCry and is never meant for the internet; many ISPs block it for that reason.
rules.advice: Close the port. Use a VPN, or a sync service, to reach files remotely.

rules.title: NetBIOS is exposed
rules.explain: NetBIOS session service leaks machine and share names and belongs on the LAN only.
rules.advice: Close the port on the router.

rules.title: An FTP server is exposed
rules.explain: An FTP server greeted WanHound. FTP sends passwords in plaintext and anonymous access is a common misconfiguration.
rules.advice: Replace FTP with SFTP or HTTPS-based sharing; if it must stay, disable anonymous login and restrict access.

rules.title: The FTP port is open
rules.explain: Port 21 is open. FTP sends passwords in plaintext.
rules.advice: Prefer SFTP; if it is FTP, disable anonymous access or close the port.

rules.title: NFS file sharing is exposed
rules.explain: NFS trusts client addresses rather than passwords; exposed exports can often be mounted by anyone.
rules.advice: Close the port and restrict exports to LAN addresses.

rules.title: rpcbind (portmapper) is exposed
rules.explain: rpcbind lists the machine's RPC services (often NFS) and is abused for DDoS amplification.
rules.advice: Block it on the router; it is only needed inside the LAN.

rules.title: An rsync daemon is exposed
rules.explain: An rsync daemon answered. Modules without auth are readable (and sometimes writable) by anyone.
rules.advice: Close the port or require auth for every module; use rsync over SSH instead.

rules.title: The rsync daemon port is open
rules.explain: Port 873 is the rsync daemon's default.
rules.advice: Require auth for every module or use rsync over SSH.

rules.title: An iSCSI storage target is exposed
rules.explain: iSCSI exposes raw disks; without CHAP it can be attached by anyone.
rules.advice: Close the port; storage protocols belong on the LAN.

rules.title: A Synology DSM default port is open
rules.explain: Ports 5000/5001 are Synology DSM's defaults, a frequent ransomware target. (On other systems 5000 may be a dev web server or AirPlay.)
rules.advice: If this is DSM: prefer QuickConnect or a VPN; otherwise HTTPS only, 2FA, auto-block, and current updates.

rules.title: The Home Assistant default port is open
rules.explain: Port 8123 is Home Assistant's default.
rules.advice: Prefer Home Assistant Cloud or a VPN; if published, HTTPS and 2FA.

rules.title: A camera video stream port (RTSP) is open
rules.explain: RTSP carries live camera video; many cameras allow stream access with default or no credentials.
rules.advice: Remove the forward/UPnP mapping; watch remotely through the vendor app or a VPN.

rules.title: An MQTT broker is exposed
rules.explain: MQTT is the message bus of many smart homes; brokers without auth let anyone read sensors and send commands.
rules.advice: Restrict the broker to the LAN, or require TLS (8883) and per-device credentials.

rules.title: An MQTT-over-TLS broker is reachable
rules.explain: The encrypted MQTT port is open; fine if every client must authenticate.
rules.advice: Verify authentication is required and anonymous access is off.

rules.title: A printer is reachable from the internet
rules.explain: Raw printing (9100) and IPP (631) let anyone print to — and sometimes reconfigure — the printer.
rules.advice: Remove the port forward/UPnP mapping; printers belong on the LAN.

rules.title: A VoIP (SIP) service is exposed
rules.explain: SIP endpoints are scanned for weak extension passwords to run up toll-fraud bills.
rules.advice: Restrict SIP to your provider's addresses, or use a VPN for remote extensions.

rules.title: A DNS server is reachable from the internet (TCP)
rules.explain: A DNS service listens on the public address. If it resolves for anyone it can be abused for amplification attacks; the UDP check tells you more.
rules.advice: Unless you host authoritative DNS on purpose, restrict the resolver to the LAN.

rules.title: A SOCKS proxy port is open
rules.explain: An open proxy lets strangers route their traffic — abuse included — through your home IP.
rules.advice: Require authentication or bind the proxy to the LAN.

rules.title: An HTTP proxy port is open
rules.explain: Port 3128 is Squid's default; an open proxy relays strangers' traffic through your IP.
rules.advice: Restrict the proxy to the LAN or require authentication.

rules.title: A PPTP VPN endpoint is exposed
rules.explain: PPTP's encryption is broken; captured logins can be cracked offline.
rules.advice: Replace PPTP with WireGuard, OpenVPN or IPsec/IKEv2.

rules.title: An OpenVPN (TCP) endpoint is reachable
rules.explain: A VPN endpoint is the right way to reach home remotely — this is usually deliberate.
rules.advice: Keep it updated and use tls-crypt/tls-auth so unauthenticated packets are dropped.

rules.title: Plex remote access is enabled
rules.explain: Plex opens this port for remote streaming, often via UPnP. It is a deliberate feature but publishes the media server.
rules.advice: Keep Plex updated and use a strong account password with 2FA; disable remote access if unused.

rules.title: A mail server port is reachable
rules.explain: Port 25 accepts mail. On a home line this is rarely intentional and, if misconfigured as an open relay, gets your IP blacklisted.
rules.advice: Close it unless you run a mail server on purpose; if you do, make sure it is not an open relay.

rules.title: An open DNS resolver is answering the internet
rules.explain: The address resolved an arbitrary name for WanHound, so it does the same for anyone — attackers use such resolvers to amplify DDoS attacks, and your line takes the blame.
rules.advice: Restrict the router's/server's DNS resolver to LAN clients only (or disable DNS on the WAN interface).

rules.title: A DNS server answers on UDP 53
rules.explain: A DNS service answers from the internet but did not resolve an arbitrary name. Fine for an authoritative server; otherwise it should be LAN-only.
rules.advice: If you do not host DNS deliberately, block UDP/TCP 53 on the WAN side.

rules.title: An NTP server answers from the internet
rules.explain: A time server answers public requests. Misconfigured NTP servers are used for DDoS amplification.
rules.advice: Unless you run a public time server, block UDP 123 inbound; make sure monlist/mode 7 is disabled.

rules.title: UPnP discovery (SSDP) answers from the internet
rules.explain: UPnP should only ever speak to the LAN. Answering on the WAN leaks device details, is abused for DDoS amplification, and on some routers lets outsiders add port mappings.
rules.advice: Disable UPnP on the WAN interface — update the router firmware, or turn UPnP off entirely.

rules.title: Multicast DNS answers from the internet
rules.explain: mDNS (Bonjour/Avahi) is a LAN-only protocol; answering on the WAN leaks device and service names and can be used for amplification.
rules.advice: Block UDP 5353 inbound on the router, or bind Avahi/Bonjour to LAN interfaces.

rules.title: An OpenVPN server answers unauthenticated packets
rules.explain: The VPN endpoint itself is fine, but it answered a session start from an unknown client, which means tls-auth/tls-crypt is not in use.
rules.advice: Enable tls-crypt (or tls-auth) so the server stays silent to anyone without the shared key.

rules.title: An IPsec VPN endpoint answers
rules.explain: An IKE daemon (IPsec VPN, often the router's built-in VPN server) is listening.
rules.advice: Fine if deliberate: keep firmware current and use IKEv2 with certificates or strong pre-shared keys.

combos.title: Your router's management is reachable from the internet
combos.explain: At least one way of administering the router or modem (web admin, TR-069, Winbox, UPnP) answers on the public side. Gateway takeovers give an attacker every device behind it.
combos.advice: In the router: disable remote/WAN management, TR-069 if the router is yours, and UPnP on WAN. Ask the ISP if the modem is theirs. Re-run WanHound to confirm.

combos.title: Remote-control or database services are published directly
combos.explain: A home line is publishing services that should only ever be reached privately. Direct exposure is what automated ransomware and botnet scanners look for.
combos.advice: Replace port forwards with a private path: a VPN on the router (WireGuard/OpenVPN), Tailscale/ZeroTier, or a tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel, frp) with authentication in front.

combos.title: Many ports are open — a DMZ host or blanket forwarding?
combos.explain: Ten or more TCP ports answer. On a home line that usually means a device is set as the router's DMZ host, or UPnP has been opening ports freely.
combos.advice: Check the router for a DMZ/exposed-host setting and the UPnP mapping table; forward only the specific ports you need.

combos.title: IPv6: open ports are the device itself
combos.explain: There is no NAT in front of an IPv6 address: every open port found here belongs directly to the device that owns this address, reachable from the whole internet.
combos.advice: Make sure the router's IPv6 firewall blocks unsolicited inbound traffic by default, and open only specific ports to specific devices.

combos.title: Smart-home or camera devices are reachable
combos.explain: IoT devices are rarely patched and are the bulk of botnet recruits. One published camera or hub can become the foothold into the home network.
combos.advice: Use vendor cloud apps or a VPN for remote access instead of port forwards; put IoT devices on a separate (guest/IoT) network.
